pos: n. pl. (the evening office of prayer and psalmody in the daily round of the hours)
etymology: Latin vesper, the evening, the evening star; cognate with Greek hesperos.
biblical_def: Vespers is the evening office, sung at the lighting of the lamps, and in the Rule of Benedict it is one of the seven day hours with Lauds, Prime, Terce, Sext, None and Compline, with Nocturns in the night. Its core is a short run of psalms, a chapter of Scripture, a hymn and the Magnificat, and it is the office most often kept where the others were let go, because it falls at a workable hour. The Reformers kept its substance: Cranmer folded Vespers and Compline together into Evening Prayer, and Reformed households kept an evening reading and psalm. This dictionary records Vespers because the practice it names is thoroughly biblical even where the machinery around it was not. Evening prayer has a direct warrant, “Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice” (Psa 141:2), and a fixed daily round is David's own habit, “Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud” (Psa 55:17). Daniel kept set hours at the cost of his life, “he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed” (Dan 6:10), and the psalmist counts his times without embarrassment, “Seven times a day do I praise thee” (Psa 119:164).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vespers as the evening service in the Romish church; evening as the latter part of the day; an hour as a canonical portion of the day for prayer; a psalm as a sacred song; and devotion as the act of worship.
webster_full: VESPERS, n. The evening song or service in the Roman Catholic church; the evening prayer or devotions.
EVENING, n. The latter part and close of the day, and the beginning of darkness or night.
HOUR, n. A certain space or portion of time; in the plural, certain prayers in the Romish church, to be repeated at stated times of the day.
PSALM, n. A sacred song or hymn; a composition in verse intended to be sung in the worship of God.
DEVOTION, n. The state of being dedicated or consecrated; piety; the performance of religious duties; prayer.
scriptures: Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice.
Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice.
Dan 6:10

Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime.
Seven times a day do I praise thee because of thy righteous judgments.
corruption_summary: The evening office: fixed daily prayer with a plain biblical warrant, kept by monasteries and by Reformed households alike.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the fixed hour. Modern prayer is almost entirely occasional, offered when a man feels like it, and Scripture's praying men were not like that. David names three set times, “Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray” (Psa 55:17); Daniel keeps his under a death sentence, “as he did aforetime” (Dan 6:10); the psalmist counts to seven, “Seven times a day do I praise thee” (Psa 119:164). A household that prays at the same hour every evening is not being monastic; it is being ordinary.

The error to avoid is treating the hour as the thing. Vespers at its worst was a quota discharged, which is the fault of a swollen liturgy rather than of fixed prayer. The image Scripture gives is not a quota but an offering carried upward, “Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense” (Psa 141:2), answered in the vision of heaven where the incense and the prayers rise together, “the smoke of the incense, which came with the prayers of the saints, ascended up before God” (Rev 8:4). Keep the hour; mind the heart in it.

pos: n. pl. (clergy living in community under the Rule of Augustine, bound to the choir office yet serving churches)
etymology: From Greek kanon, a measuring rod, a rule; with Latin regularis, living under a rule.
biblical_def: Canons regular are ordained clergy who live in community under a rule, chiefly the Rule of Augustine, and who keep the choir office as monks do while also serving churches, schools and hospitals. They emerged in the eleventh century out of reforming efforts to make cathedral and collegiate clergy live in common and hold no private property, and the Premonstratensians are their most famous order. The distinction from monks is substantial: a monk is a layman by origin whose business is his own sanctification within an enclosure, whereas a canon is a cleric whose business is public ministry. This dictionary records the canons because their hybrid is the nearest medieval approach to the New Testament's arrangement and because the gap that remains is the point. Scripture knows ordained men gathered in colleges of elders, “ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23), devoted to the word and to prayer rather than to administration, “give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word” (Act 6:4). It also knows these men as householders, “A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife” (1Ti 3:2). The canons took the college and the office and the ministry, and kept the one vow Scripture never imposes, so the household went missing, “Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled” (Heb 13:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a canon as a church dignitary holding a prebend; regular as governed by rule; a college as a collection of persons with common duties; a cleric as one in holy orders; and community as common possession or society.
webster_full: CANON, n. A dignitary of the church; a person who possesses a prebend or revenue allotted for the performance of divine service in a cathedral or collegiate church.
REGULAR, adj. Governed by rule or rules; instituted or initiated according to established forms or discipline.
COLLEGE, n. In a general sense, a collection or assemblage; a society of men invested with certain powers, performing certain duties, or engaged in some common employment.
CLERICAL, adj. Relating to the clergy; as clerical errors; pertaining to a clerk or writer.
COMMUNITY, n. Common possession; as a community of goods; also, society at large, or a body of people having common rights.
scriptures: And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
Act 6:4
But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word.
A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
Heb 13:4
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
corruption_summary: Clergy in community under rule: the medieval arrangement closest to a college of elders, less the households Scripture assumes.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the college itself. Scripture does not leave a minister alone with a congregation; it appoints a body of men together, “ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23), and it guards their time for the work that only they can do, “give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word” (Act 6:4). The canons built a structure that assumed clergy need one another, which is more than many modern churches assume.

The remaining error is the vow. Paul assumes an overseer has a wife and children and judges him partly by how he governs them, “the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour” (1Ti 3:2); a rule that forbids him the household removes the very evidence the apostle asks for. Where Scripture calls a thing honourable, “Marriage is honourable in all” (Heb 13:4), a rule that forbids it is a departure rather than a discipline, “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats” (1Ti 4:3).

pos: n. (a professed member of a monastery bound to manual labour rather than to the choir office)
etymology: Lay, from Greek laos, the people, through Latin laicus; with brother.
biblical_def: A lay brother was a professed religious who took the vows and wore the habit but was not ordained, did not sing the full choir office, and was assigned the manual work of the house: the fields, the forge, the flocks, the granges. The Cistercians developed the institution on a vast scale, because their Rule required manual labour and their choir monks could not both farm thousands of acres and keep a lengthy office. Lay brothers were often illiterate by design, said simple prayers instead of the psalter, ate and slept apart, and had no vote in chapter. At some houses they outnumbered the choir monks three to one, and more than once they rebelled. This dictionary records the lay brother because the arrangement is a clean illustration of a division Scripture refuses. The work he did is honourable without qualification, “let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good” (Eph 4:28), “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might” (Ecc 9:10). But a two-tier brotherhood, where one class prays and another digs, contradicts the levelling the gospel works, “there is neither bond nor free” (Gal 3:28), and the plain word that the lower seat is where greatness is found, “whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister” (Mat 20:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lay as pertaining to the people as distinct from the clergy; a brother as one closely united to another; labour as bodily exertion; a servant as one who attends another; and a degree as a step or rank in order.
webster_full: LAY, adj. Pertaining to the laity or people, in distinction from the clergy; not clerical; as a lay person; a lay preacher.
BROTHER, n. A term of great breadth, denoting one closely united to another; an associate; one of the same profession, society or kindred.
LABOR, n. Exertion of muscular strength, or bodily exertion which occasions weariness; particularly, the exertion of the limbs in occupations by which subsistence is obtained.
SERVANT, n. A person, male or female, that attends another for the purpose of performing menial offices for him.
DEGREE, n. A step; a rank or station in life; a measure of advancement; as a man of high degree.
scriptures: Eph 4:28
Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.
Ecc 9:10
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
Gal 3:28
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;
corruption_summary: The unlettered working religious of the Cistercian granges: labour honoured in fact and demoted in rank.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of the work itself, which the institution both relied on and undervalued. Scripture attaches no second rank to hands, “working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth” (Eph 4:28), and it commands wholeheartedness in whatever work comes, “do it with thy might” (Ecc 9:10). The granges fed Europe; the men who worked them were kept from the psalter.

The error is the grading of brothers. The gospel does the opposite, abolishing the categories in which a man is ranked before God, “there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female” (Gal 3:28), and Christ places greatness at the bottom of the arrangement rather than the top, “let him be your minister” (Mat 20:26). A monastery that kept its workers illiterate so they would not need the choir had built its own rebellion into the walls, and it came.

“let him be your minister” (Mat 20:26) — greatness located where the lay brother already stood.

pos: n. pl. (Latin, the converted: adult recruits to a monastery, and especially the lay brothers of the Cistercians)
etymology: Latin conversi, plural of conversus, turned about, converted.
biblical_def: Conversi is the Latin term for those who entered a monastery as adults, by conversion of life, as distinct from the nutriti who had been given to the house as children and raised in it. Among the Cistercians the word settled onto the lay brothers specifically, and the liber usuum conversorum regulated their day. The distinction matters historically because it marks a real change: early medieval monasteries were filled largely by child oblates, whereas the twelfth-century reform orders drew grown men who chose it, often knights, merchants and peasants with a life behind them. This dictionary records the word because the thing it names, a turning of the whole life, is the Bible's own category, and because the medieval usage narrowed it badly. Scripture calls conversion a turning of the heart to God, “rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God” (Joe 2:13), and makes it the condition of entering the kingdom at all rather than a monastery, “Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 18:3). It is not a change of address or clothing. The new man is created, not enrolled, “if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature” (2Co 5:17), and the turning is God's work before it is ours, “a great number believed, and turned unto the Lord” (Act 11:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conversion as a change of heart in which enmity to God is subdued; to convert as to turn from one state to another; a novice as one newly admitted; profession as the act of avowing; and regeneration as new birth by the Spirit.
webster_full: CONVERSION, n. In a theological or moral sense, a change of heart, or dispositions, in which the enmity of the heart to God is subdued, and is succeeded by love.
CONVERT, v.t. To change or turn from one state to another; to turn from one religion or sect to another; to turn from a bad life to a good one.
NOVICE, n. One who is new in any business; one unacquainted or unskilled; one newly admitted to membership in a religious house.
PROFESSION, n. The act of professing or avowing; open declaration; also, the business which one professes to understand and to follow.
REGENERATION, n. New birth by the grace of God; that change by which the will and natural enmity of man to God is subdued, and a principle of love is implanted.
scriptures: Joe 2:13
And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil.
Mat 18:3
And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.
Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
And the hand of the Lord was with them: and a great number believed, and turned unto the Lord.
corruption_summary: Latin for the converted, narrowed by the Cistercians to the working brothers: a biblical word made into a class of men.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the word's full force. Conversion in Scripture is interior and total, and the prophet rules out the gesture that substitutes for it, “rend your heart, and not your garments” (Joe 2:13). A habit is a garment. The Cistercian conversus had genuinely turned in many cases, and the term still described his paperwork rather than his heart.

The live misuse today is the opposite narrowing: conversion treated as a decision recorded at a meeting. Christ makes it the gate of the kingdom and describes it as becoming small, “Except ye be converted, and become as little children” (Mat 18:3); Paul makes it a new creation rather than a new category, “old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new” (2Co 5:17); and Luke reports it as a turning to a person, “a great number believed, and turned unto the Lord” (Act 11:21). Neither a monastery nor a card can manufacture it.

pos: n. (the room in a monastery set apart for copying manuscripts)
etymology: Late Latin scriptorium, a place for writing, from scribere, to write.
biblical_def: A scriptorium is the writing room of a monastery, where monks copied, corrected, illuminated and bound manuscripts. The work was cold, slow and exacting: a scribe ruled his parchment, cut and recut his quill, held a knife in his left hand to steady the skin and scrape errors, and could manage a few leaves in a day. Cassiodorus at Vivarium in the sixth century made copying an explicit act of devotion, and Benedictine houses carried the practice for a thousand years, which is the single reason most Latin literature and the Latin Bible reached the age of printing at all. This dictionary records the scriptorium with real gratitude, because the labour it names is biblical in a direct way. Scripture is a written thing by God's own command, “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2), “Now go, write it before them in a table, and note it in a book” (Isa 30:8). A king was required to make his own copy and read it for life, “And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life” (Deu 17:19). Even an apostle in prison wanted his books brought, “bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a scribe as a writer, and among the Jews a teacher of the law; a manuscript as a book written by hand; parchment as the skin of a sheep prepared for writing; a copy as a transcript; and to transcribe as to copy.
webster_full: SCRIBE, n. A writer; a notary; a public writer; among the Jews, a clerk or secretary, and a teacher or interpreter of the law.
MANUSCRIPT, n. A book or paper written with the hand or pen; a writing of any kind, in distinction from what is printed.
PARCHMENT, n. The skin of a sheep or goat dressed and prepared for writing.
COPY, n. A writing like another writing; a transcript from an original; hence, a book, as a copy of the Bible.
TRANSCRIBE, v.t. To copy; to write over again or in the same words; to write a copy of any thing.
scriptures: Hab 2:2
And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
Isa 30:8
Now go, write it before them in a table, and note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come for ever and ever:
And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them:
The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments.
corruption_summary: The monastic writing room: the labour that carried the text of Scripture through a thousand years, and a debt Protestants seldom acknowledge.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the written-ness of revelation. God commands his word put into legible form for a running reader, “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables” (Hab 2:2), and ordered for the distant future, “that it may be for the time to come for ever and ever” (Isa 30:8). A faith that is content with impressions has lost something the scriptorium understood with its knife and quill.

The temptation to name is ingratitude dressed as discernment. Protestants who rightly reject medieval doctrine sometimes speak as though the centuries between the apostles and the Reformation were a void, when in fact unnamed monks were copying the very text the Reformers would preach from. Scripture itself honours the care of books, “especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13), and requires a personal copy read for a lifetime, “that he may learn to fear the LORD his God” (Deu 17:19). Thank the copyists; correct the doctrine.

pos: n. (the hall of a monastery in which the community eats together)
etymology: Late Latin refectorium, a place of refreshment, from reficere, to restore.
biblical_def: The refectory is the dining hall of a religious house, and the Rule of Benedict regulates it closely: the brethren eat together at fixed hours, in silence, while one of them reads aloud from a raised desk so that the mind is fed with the body. The reader was changed weekly and asked a blessing before beginning; signs replaced speech for passing bread. Two cooked dishes were allowed, with fruit when available, a pound of bread for the day, and a measure of wine conceded with a shrug at human weakness. This dictionary records the refectory because the common table is one of the oldest and plainest marks of the church, and because the silence imposed on it is a loss rather than a gain. Eating together is apostolic practice, “breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart” (Act 2:46), and it is explicitly glad. The reading aloud at table answers a real need, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God” (Mat 4:4). But the table in Scripture is a place of speech, where men talk and are known, and the common life it serves is a shared one, “they had all things common” (Act 4:32), “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” (Heb 13:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a refectory as a room for refreshment or meals; a repast as a meal; to refresh as to revive after fatigue; bread as food made of flour; and a table as an article of furniture on which meat is served.
webster_full: REFECTORY, n. A room of refreshment; a place where refreshments are taken; usually, a hall in convents and monasteries where the monks take their meals.
REPAST, n. The act of taking food; or the food taken; a meal.
REFRESH, v.t. To cool; to allay heat; to revive after fatigue or exhaustion; to give new strength or vigor.
BREAD, n. Food made of flour or meal; also, food in general; support of life.
TABLE, n. An article of furniture consisting of a flat surface supported on legs; also, fare or entertainment; as, he keeps a good table.
scriptures: Act 2:46
And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart,
Mat 4:4
But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.
Act 4:32
And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.
Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
corruption_summary: The monastic dining hall: the common table kept faithfully, under a silence the apostolic table did not know.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the common table itself, which the modern household has largely lost to screens and separate hours. The first Christians ate together constantly and the text notices their faces, “did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart” (Act 2:46). The monks were right that meals are formative; a family that never sits down together is forming something too.

The reform needed is in the silence. Reading at table is a good custom, and the sentence behind it is true, “but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God” (Mat 4:4). But Scripture's meals are talking meals, where strangers are received and known, “for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb 13:2), and where a community's actual sharing is visible, “neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own” (Act 4:32). A rule that silences the table protects recollection and costs fellowship.

pos: n. (the room where a monastic community assembles daily for business, correction and the reading of the rule)
etymology: From Latin capitulum, a little head, a chapter of a book, because a chapter of the rule was read there.
biblical_def: The chapter house is the assembly room of a monastery, usually east of the cloister, and it takes its name from the chapter of the Rule read aloud there each morning. After the reading came the business of the house: the abbot's instruction, the assignment of work, the commemoration of the dead, and the chapter of faults, in which brethren accused themselves and were accused of breaches of the Rule and received correction before the whole community. Elections were held there and the seal kept there. This dictionary records the chapter house because its central practice, open and regular correction among brothers, is commanded in Scripture and almost entirely absent from modern church life. Correction is to be faithful rather than flattering, “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Pro 27:6), and it is to be done in the open where sin is public, “Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear” (1Ti 5:20). The Lord lays out the steps himself, ending with the assembly, “tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17). The whole aim is restoration rather than punishment, and it is to be done gently by those who are themselves watching, “restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Gal 6:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chapter as an assembly of ecclesiastics; discipline as instruction and government; to rebuke as to chide or reprove; correction as amendment; and an assembly as a company met together.
webster_full: CHAPTER, n. An assembly of the clergy of a cathedral or collegiate church, or of the members of a religious order; also, a division of a book.
DISCIPLINE, n. Instruction and government, comprehending the communication of knowledge and the regulation of practice.
REBUKE, v.t. To chide; to reprove; to reprehend for a fault; to check or restrain by expression of disapprobation.
CORRECTION, n. The act of correcting; amendment; rectification; also, punishment intended to amend.
ASSEMBLY, n. A company of persons collected together in one place, and usually for some common purpose.
scriptures: Pro 27:6
Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear.
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Gal 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
corruption_summary: The daily assembly room of a monastery: regular brotherly correction practised faithfully, and almost lost to the modern church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the practice itself. A community that meets daily to hear its rule and name its faults has something most congregations have quietly abandoned. Scripture treats correction as an act of love with a cost attached, “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Pro 27:6), and sets public sin in the open, “Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear” (1Ti 5:20).

The live corruption is the modern conviction that any correction is an assault on the person. That idea cannot be squared with the Lord's own procedure, which escalates patiently and ends in the assembly, “tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17). The guardrail Scripture supplies is not silence but meekness and self-suspicion in the corrector, “considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Gal 6:1). A church with no chapter of faults has not become kinder; it has only become quieter about the same sins.

Greek katartizo (G2675) — to mend, to set a bone, to restore; “restore such an one in the spirit of meekness”, Galatians 6:1.

“tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17) — the assembly as the last step, not the first.
“considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Gal 6:1) — the clause that keeps correction from cruelty.

pos: n. (an outlying farm of a monastery, worked by lay brothers; by extension, a granary or farmstead)
etymology: Old French grange, a barn, from Latin granica, a granary, from granum, grain.
biblical_def: A grange was the outlying farm of a monastic estate, with its own barns, byres, chapel and dormitory for the lay brothers who worked it, placed a day's travel or less from the abbey so that the brethren could return for the great feasts. The Cistercians raised the grange into a system. Forbidden to hold manors and tithes, they farmed directly instead, and their granges drained fens, cleared forest, ran enormous flocks and made the order the largest wool producer in England. The word later loosened into any farmhouse with its barns. This dictionary records the grange because it is an honest picture of productive labour under a vow of poverty, and because Scripture has a settled view of barns. Filling them is a blessing, “So shall thy barns be filled with plenty” (Pro 3:10), and it is God who gives the increase rather than the system, “neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase” (1Co 3:7). But a full barn is also the setting of the Lord's hardest parable about security, “I will pull down my barns, and build greater” (Luk 12:18), and the estate the Cistercians built eventually did to them what it did to the rich fool, “a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth” (Luk 12:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a grange as a farm with its buildings; a barn as a covered building for grain; a granary as a storehouse for threshed grain; husbandry as the business of a farmer; and tillage as the operation of ploughing and preparing ground.
webster_full: GRANGE, n. A farm, with the buildings, stables, etc., belonging to it; properly, a farm house with barns, granaries and other conveniences.
BARN, n. A covered building for securing grain, hay, flax, and other productions of the earth.
GRANARY, n. A storehouse or repository of grain after it is threshed; a corn house.
HUSBANDRY, n. The business of a farmer, comprehending agriculture or tillage of the ground, the raising, managing and fattening of cattle and other domestic animals.
TILLAGE, n. The operation, practice or art of tilling and preparing land for seed, and keeping the ground free from weeds.
scriptures: Pro 3:10
So shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy presses shall burst out with new wine.
So then neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase.
And he said, This will I do: I will pull down my barns, and build greater; and there will I bestow all my fruits and my goods.
And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
corruption_summary: The outlying monastic farm: poverty vowed and plenty produced, until the barns did to the order what they did to the rich fool.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that honest farming is blessed work and that the increase is God's to give. Scripture connects a full barn with God's favour rather than man's cleverness, “So shall thy barns be filled with plenty” (Pro 3:10), and strips the labourer of any claim to the harvest, “but God that giveth the increase” (1Co 3:7). The Cistercian grange was genuinely good work.

The live warning is what the barns did next. An order founded in a marsh to escape wealth became, through sheer competence, immensely wealthy, and the wealth dissolved the discipline exactly as it had at Cluny and Molesme. The Lord's parable is precisely about a man whose solution to abundance is more storage, “I will pull down my barns, and build greater” (Luk 12:18), and the verse that introduces it is the one the order needed on the lintel of every grange, “Take heed, and beware of covetousness” (Luk 12:15).

Greek auxano (G837) — to cause to grow, to give the increase; “but God that giveth the increase”, 1 Corinthians 3:7.
Greek apotheke (G596) — a storehouse, a barn; “I will pull down my barns, and build greater”, Luke 12:18.
Greek pleonexia (G4124) — the greed that always wants more; “Take heed, and beware of covetousness”, Luke 12:15.

“I will pull down my barns, and build greater” (Luk 12:18) — the parable the granges eventually enacted.
“but God that giveth the increase” (1Co 3:7) — who the harvest actually belongs to.

pos: n. (one who withdraws from the world to a solitary cell, often walled into a cell attached to a church)
etymology: Greek anachoretes, one who has retired, from anachorein, to withdraw.
biblical_def: An anchorite, or in the feminine an anchoress, is a solitary who withdraws permanently from ordinary society, and in the medieval West the term came to mean specifically one enclosed in a cell built against the wall of a church, with a squint looking onto the altar, a window to a servant, and a window to the street for counsel. The rite of enclosure borrowed the office for the dead. Julian of Norwich is the best known English anchoress; the Ancrene Wisse was written to guide three such women. This dictionary records the anchorite because the practice presses an unusual question: how far may withdrawal go before it becomes disobedience? Scripture records genuine solitaries whom God himself sent into the waste, “hide thyself by the brook Cherith, that is before Jordan” (1Ki 17:3), and commends those driven out by persecution, “they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth” (Heb 11:38). But these are men placed there by providence rather than men who walled themselves in, and the ordinary shape of obedience is a visible life among neighbours, “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works” (Mat 5:16), doing good as opportunity comes, “As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men” (Gal 6:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an anchoret as a hermit who retires from society; a recluse as one shut up from the world; a cell as the hut of a hermit; seclusion as separation from society; and contemplation as holy meditation.
webster_full: ANCHORET, n. A hermit; a recluse; one who retires from society into a desert or solitary place, to avoid the temptations of the world and devote himself to religious duties.
RECLUSE, adj. Shut up; sequestered; retired from the world or from public notice; solitary.
CELL, n. A small or close apartment, as in a prison; also, a small cave or hollow place; the cave or hut of a hermit.
SECLUSION, n. The act of separating from society or connection; the state of being separate or apart; retirement; privacy.
CONTEMPLATION, n. Holy meditation; attention to sacred things; a particular attention to the subject of our salvation.
scriptures: Get thee hence, and turn thee eastward, and hide thyself by the brook Cherith, that is before Jordan.
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Mat 5:16
Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
Gal 6:10
As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.
corruption_summary: The walled-in solitary: a real biblical wilderness made into a permanent vocation, and a light set under a wall.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture's solitaries are sent, not self-dispatched. Elijah is given a destination and a brook by direct command, “Get thee hence, and turn thee eastward, and hide thyself by the brook Cherith” (1Ki 17:3), and the wanderers of Hebrews are fugitives from persecution rather than volunteers, “they wandered in deserts, and in mountains” (Heb 11:38). Providence may put a believer in a cave; a believer should be slow to build one.

The live error is the assumption that holiness is chiefly a matter of removal. The Lord assumes visibility instead, “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works” (Mat 5:16), and the apostle makes the field of obedience the people one actually encounters, “let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith” (Gal 6:10). The anchoress counselling through her street window was closer to this than the rite of enclosure intended, and that window is the best thing in the whole arrangement.

Greek planao (G4105) — to wander, driven rather than choosing; “they wandered in deserts, and in mountains”, Hebrews 11:38.
Greek lampo (G2989) — to shine out where it is seen; “Let your light so shine before men”, Matthew 5:16.
Greek kairos (G2540) — a season, an opportunity to act; “As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men”, Galatians 6:10.
Greek spelaion (G4693) — a cave, the refuge of the persecuted; “and in dens and caves of the earth”, Hebrews 11:38.

“they wandered in deserts, and in mountains” (Heb 11:38) — fugitives, not volunteers.
“Let your light so shine before men” (Mat 5:16) — the visibility a walled cell forfeits.

pos: n. (a monk who lives in community under a rule, as distinguished from a solitary)
etymology: Greek koinobion, common life, from koinos, common, and bios, life.
biblical_def: A cenobite is a monk of the common life, living in a community under a rule and an abbot, and the word stands in deliberate contrast to the hermit or anchorite. Pachomius in fourth-century Egypt organised the first great cenobitic houses, giving solitaries a wall, a timetable and a superior, and Benedict two centuries later opened his Rule by naming the cenobites the strongest kind of monk and the kind he writes for. The Greek behind the term is the New Testament's own word for the shared life. This dictionary records the cenobite because the instinct is right even where the institution is not. The church is by definition a common life, and the first one is described in exactly these terms, “the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul” (Act 4:32), with its goods held loosely, “all that believed were together, and had all things common” (Act 2:44). Companionship is treated as strength rather than compromise, “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour” (Ecc 4:9). What Scripture does not do is confine that common life to a cloister: the household, the congregation and the table are where it is meant to happen, “how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Psa 133:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cenobite as one who lives in community with others; a convent as a body of monks or nuns; common as belonging equally to more than one; unity as concord; and society as a number of persons united by mutual consent.
webster_full: CENOBITE, n. One of a religious order, who live in a convent or in community, in opposition to an anchoret or hermit, who lives in solitude.
CONVENT, n. An assembly of persons devoted to religion; a body of monks or nuns; also, the house occupied by such a society.
COMMON, adj. Belonging equally to more than one, or to many indefinitely; usual; general; of no rank.
UNITY, n. The state of being one; concord; conjunction; agreement; uniformity.
SOCIETY, n. The union of a number of rational beings; a number of persons united, either for a temporary purpose or by the bonds of a common interest.
scriptures: Act 4:32
And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.
Act 2:44
And all that believed were together, and had all things common;
Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
A Song of degrees of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
corruption_summary: The monk of the common life: the right instinct that Christians are made for one another, confined to a cloister Scripture never builds.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the instinct itself. Christianity is not a solitary religion, and the first church is described in language the cenobites borrowed directly, “of one heart and of one soul” (Act 4:32). Even the wisdom literature argues the case practically, “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour” (Ecc 4:9), and adds that the bound strand holds, “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecc 4:12).

The error is the enclosure, not the fellowship. Scripture locates the common life in households, congregations and shared tables rather than behind a gate, “all that believed were together, and had all things common” (Act 2:44), and the psalm that every monastery quoted is about brethren dwelling together without specifying a cloister, “how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Psa 133:1). A congregation that knows one another has more of what the cenobite wanted than most cloisters managed.

Greek koinos (G2839) — common, shared by all; “and had all things common”, Acts 2:44.
Hebrew sakar (H7939) — a reward, wages for shared labour; “because they have a good reward for their labour”, Ecclesiastes 4:9.
Hebrew yachad (H3162) — together, in union; “for brethren to dwell together in unity”, Psalm 133:1.
Hebrew chebel (H2256) — a cord, strength in the twisting; “a threefold cord is not quickly broken”, Ecclesiastes 4:12.
usage: “of one heart and of one soul” (Act 4:32) — the common life the cenobites were imitating.
“Two are better than one” (Ecc 4:9) — the plain argument against the hermit's cell.
“for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Psa 133:1) — the psalm every cloister claimed, which names no cloister.
